archetype.name: Playoff Team (defense-first)
archetype.definition: A Macdonald team whose top-five defense carries a below-average, turnover-prone offense to a winning record, good enough to make the field but thin enough that one sloppy afternoon flips a game.

report.headline: Elite defense, leaky offense: Seattle's losses come from its own giveaways
report.take:
Seattle is still, at heart, last year's team on defense. The 2025 unit ranked 1st in EPA allowed, and this one sits 5th. It is 1st in yards allowed per game, 2nd in success rate allowed, and 1st in explosive pass rate allowed. Macdonald's group doesn't give up big plays, gets home with pressure (5th in pressure rate, 3rd in QB hit rate), and gets off the field on third down (3rd). That is the engine of a 6-4 record built on a +48 point differential. The differential implies 6.9 wins, so if anything Seattle has been a bit unlucky (winsOverExpected -0.94).

The offense is the drag, and it has two separate problems. The first is self-inflicted: 16 turnovers and a turnover margin of -0.6 a game, 26th in the league. The four losses read like a ledger of giveaways. Three turnovers at Washington, four against San Francisco and three at Denver produced three one-score losses, two of them as the favorite. All came in Drew Lock's stretch of starts. The second problem is structural. The run game is 29th in rush EPA and 27th in short-yardage conversion, yet the staff still runs well above expectation (pass rate over expected -6.9, 29th). Meanwhile the passing game is quietly respectable at 13th in pass EPA. Seattle is leaning on its weaker half.

What the raw numbers hide is a bend-at-the-goal-line flaw on defense. Opponents rarely move the ball, but when they reach the red zone they score touchdowns 75% of the time (29th). Short passing is also the soft spot (23rd in short-pass EPA allowed, against 2nd on deep balls). The other thing the numbers hide is the quarterback split. Darnold's starts have produced cleaner football, including positive pass EPA in three of his four starts. Most of the turnover damage came with Lock.

Coming out of the bye, the path forward depends on health. Darnold, both starting tackles and Quenton Nelson all carry Nov. 29 return estimates. The remaining schedule beyond San Francisco includes Dallas's 32nd-ranked defense and a 2-7 Philadelphia. That is a softer stretch than the record so far suggests. A team that keeps its giveaways near league average with this defense is a double-digit-win team. One that doesn't stays stuck in a three-way scramble with the Rams.

strengths.title: A defense that erases explosive plays
strengths.body: Seattle allows the lowest rate of explosive passes in the league and ranks 2nd against deep throws. That forces offenses to string together long drives, and few manage it: the defense is 2nd in success rate allowed. This is a scheme identity rather than a hot streak, since the 2025 defense led the league in EPA allowed. Expect it to hold.

strengths.title: Pressure without blitz-heavy risk
strengths.body: The front ranks 5th in pressure rate and 3rd in QB hit rate. It peaked with six sacks in Las Vegas. Pressure is a big reason opponents can't push the ball downfield. The one caveat is depth: Leonard Williams is out with a stinger and Jarran Reed is questionable, which tests how much of this survives on the interior.

strengths.title: A passing game better than its reputation
strengths.body: Despite the league's worst pressure rate allowed, Seattle is 13th in pass EPA. Jaxon Smith-Njigba commands a dominant share with 109 targets, and Darnold's starts produced strong passing days like the Kansas City win. The offense would likely be better served throwing more than it does.

concerns.title: Giveaways decide the losses
concerns.body: Sixteen turnovers have wiped out what should be a cushion from the defense. The three-plus-turnover games at Washington, against San Francisco and at Denver were all one-score losses. Most of the damage came in Lock's starts, so Darnold's health is the biggest lever. Turnover margins also tend to drift back toward neutral, which favors Seattle from here.

concerns.title: A run game that doesn't earn its volume
concerns.body: Seattle is 29th in rush EPA and 27th in short-yardage success. Yards before contact are middle of the pack, so the backs and the blocking at the point of attack share the blame. The line is also last in pressure rate allowed, and three starters (Nelson, Cross, Lucas) are injured. Unless that group comes back healthy, the ground game isn't going to fix itself.

concerns.title: Red zone and underneath leaks
concerns.body: Seattle's defense rarely gives ground, but inside the 20 it allows touchdowns at the 4th-worst rate in the league. It is also only 23rd against short passes. That is the cost of a shell built to deny explosives: patient offenses can dink their way down and finish. Against good offenses this is where points sneak through.

trend.note: The turnover-riddled run of one-score losses came in late September and October. Since then Seattle has won its last two, holding Arizona to 3 and Las Vegas to 13, with cleaner quarterback play. The Chicago blowout is the reminder that the floor is still low when the offense stalls.

nextGame.headline: At 8-1 San Francisco, with Seattle's line and QB in question
nextGame.body:
This is the league's No. 1 offense by EPA against a top-five defense, and the matchup sets up largely in San Francisco's favor. The 49ers are 1st in pass EPA and 1st in success rate. Behind them is the best pass protection in the league by sack rate, which blunts Seattle's main defensive weapon. The underneath game should be there for them against a Seattle defense that is soft on short throws. San Francisco's defense, by contrast, is built to stop exactly what Seattle likes to do: it is 1st in rush EPA allowed and 1st in explosive run rate allowed. It is vulnerable through the air, though, ranking 31st in sack rate and 24th against short passes. Seattle lost the first meeting 32-29 at home with four turnovers. The 49ers' record also carries some fortune: they are perfect in one-score games and among the league's leaders in wins over expected. No line is posted yet.

Availability is the swing. Seattle comes off a bye with Darnold, Charles Cross, Quenton Nelson and Leonard Williams all listed out, with return estimates of the game date. The coach is "really optimistic" Darnold practices fully and starts. Abraham Lucas and Jarran Reed are questionable. If both tackles and Nelson miss, a line that already allows the most pressure in the league is badly exposed, even against a modest pass rush. San Francisco is thin in the secondary, with Renardo Green questionable and Nate Hobbs on IR. It has also lost interior linemen Gracen Halton and C.J. West to IR, and Mike Evans is out but hoping to practice.

waysToWin.title: Throw it, not run it
waysToWin.body: San Francisco's run defense is elite, but its pass defense is average and its rush is among the league's weakest by sack rate. A healthy Darnold feeding Smith-Njigba can attack a secondary missing bodies. Opposing WR1s have outscored their usual output against this defense. Seattle has to override its run-heavy habits to cash this in.

waysToWin.title: Make Purdy drive the whole field
waysToWin.body: Seattle allows the fewest explosive passes and is 2nd against deep throws. San Francisco must earn points in long sequences, and Seattle's 3rd-ranked third-down defense gets several chances per drive to end them. Holding the 49ers under their scoring pace starts with no cheap chunk plays.

waysToWin.title: Win the hidden yardage
waysToWin.body: Seattle is 5th in special-teams EPA a game; San Francisco is dead last. Seattle also goes for it on fourth down more readily than anyone. Field position and extra possessions are a realistic way for the less efficient team to steal a divisional road game.

waysToLose.title: Another turnover giveaway
waysToLose.body: The first meeting turned on four Seattle turnovers. San Francisco ranks 5th in takeaways, and Seattle's turnover margin is among the league's worst. A short field for the No. 1 offense is the fastest way for this to get away.

waysToLose.title: Stubborn running into a wall
waysToLose.body: Seattle's run game is 29th in EPA, and San Francisco's run defense is 1st. If the offense keeps feeding the run on early downs, it will face long third downs behind a patched line that already allows the most pressure in the league. That leads to stalled drives and a time-of-possession war Seattle can't win.

waysToLose.title: Dinked to death, then finished
waysToLose.body: San Francisco leads the league in offensive success rate, and Seattle's weak spots are short passes and red-zone defense. A methodical 49ers attack can turn Seattle's no-explosives shell into a series of long touchdown drives.

nextGame.watch: Who lines up at quarterback and both tackle spots. A healthy Darnold behind Cross and Lucas makes this a competitive pass-first game; Lock behind backups makes it the Week 5 turnover game again.

restOfSeason.body:
The defense is the sustainable part. It has carried over from a league-best 2025 and should keep Seattle in nearly every game. The turnover margin is the part most likely to improve, both because such margins regress and because Darnold's return should clean it up. The point differential already says this team has played a bit better than its record. The schedule after San Francisco helps: Dallas, the Giants, Philadelphia and Carolina are all winnable, with Dallas fielding the league's worst defense. That leaves the two Rams games, against the 3rd-ranked defense, likely deciding seeding.

The ceiling is capped by the offense. A bottom-five run game and a line that leaks pressure won't suddenly become strengths. The red-zone defense also invites close games against good offenses. Expect a winning finish and a wild-card-level team. The division looks out of reach with San Francisco at 8-1 unless Seattle wins in Santa Clara.
swingFactors: Return of Cross, Nelson and Lucas on the line
The two late games against the Rams

confidence.note: The defense's profile is stable across two seasons, but the quarterback split and line injuries make the offense hard to pin down.
